Athlone Urban 
Area Plan (JUAP) 
Work progressed on the preparation of the chapters of the Draft  Plan.  
 
The Planning Department are currently engaging with the Department of 
Housing, Local Government and Heritage with a view to establishing the 
statutory requirements associated with the provisions of the Planning Act 
that came into force on 31 December 2025 (Planning and Development 
Act 2024 (Commencement) (No. 5) Order 2025 (S.I. No. 633/2025)) in 
relation to Development Plans and Coordinated Area Plans. A joint update 
will be provided to both councils in this regard in the coming weeks.  
 
A Settlement Capacity Audit (SCA) has been undertaken which serves as 
an evidence base for the AJUAP. The audit provides a comprehensive 
assessment of Athlone and Monksland/Bellanamullia, evaluating their 
infrastructural capacity to accommodate projected population growth, 
housing demand and economic development over the Plan's 10-year 
lifetime. Adopting a Tiered Zoning approach, the SCA categorises zoned 
lands into distinct tiers based on development readiness. Tier 1 
encompasses serviced lands with existing infrastructure capacity suitable 
for immediate development, while Tier 2 comprises un-serviced lands 
necessitating substantial investment before development can proceed. 
 
The SCA’s findings will directly inform the Plan's strategic zoning of both 
residential and employment-generating land uses and the draft chapters 
will reflect this zoning strategy.

Westmeath Age Friendly Strategy 
Westmeath County Council launched the Westmeath Age Friendly 
Strategy 2025–2028 on December 1st in Bloomfield House Hotel, 
reaffirming its commitment to creating a county where people of all 
ages can live well, feel valued and stay connected. The Strategy 
brings together key agencies, community and service providers to 
collaborate on improving the lives of older people in Westmeath. 
The Strategy represents a co-ordinated, cross-sector initiative, led by Westmeath County 
Council, ensuring a unified and strategic approach to advancing age friendly actions. 
Built on consultation with over 70 community, voluntary and older people’s groups, the 
Strategy aligns with the National Positive Ageing Strategy and the World Health 
Organisation’s Global Age Friendly Cities initiative, with a focus on improvements in eight 
key areas: 
o Outdoor spaces & buildings 
o Transport 
o Housing 
o Respect & social inclusion 
o Social participation 
o Communication & information 
o Civic participation & employment 
o Community support & health services

event on separate listings.

and deliver a two-day Samhain festival. Although very challenging given wet weather 
conditions and parking challenges, this festival was delivered with great success, strong

storytelling event followed by a fire display at the Jealous Wall. Other smaller event organisers

Speed Limit Review: 
The Road Traffic Act 2024 provides for the phased lowering of speed limits in Ireland.  
 
Phase 1.      A reduction in the default speed limit on rural local roads from 80km/h to 60km/h.   
Phase 2.     The introduction of a 30km/h speed limit in built-up and urban areas.   
Phase 3.     A reduction in the speed limit on national secondary roads from 100km/h to 80km/h. 
 
The first phase, the change in the default speed limit on rural local roads from 80km/h to 60km/h 
commenced in 2024 and this lowered default speed limit came into effect on the 7th February , 2025.   
 
 
In 2024, Westmeath County Council completed a review in accordance with section 9 of the Road 
Traffic Act of 2004, for our rural local roads. Following completion of this first phase review, no 
amendments to the existing byelaws were required; the new national default speed limit of 60km/h 
was applied to all our rural local roads.  
 
The second phase of the proposed speed limit changes concerns the introduction of a 30km/h speed 
limit in urban areas. It is intended that this speed limit change will be introduced by way of ‘special 
speed limit bye-laws’, rather than a change in the ‘default speed limit’. Accordingly, in respect of 
those roads in urban areas where local authorities propose to change existing speed limits to 30km/h, 
it will be necessary for each local authority to undertake a statutory public consultation process and 
consider representations, in accordance with the requirements of the ‘Road Traffic Act 2004’, as 
amended. As the making of ‘special speed limit bye-laws’ is a reserved function, the speed limits on 
roads in urban areas will only be changed where a majority of the elected members vote to do so. 
To assist local authorities with the process of setting ‘special speed limits’ in urban areas and the 
attendant bye-laws procedures, a working group is presently revising the ‘Guidelines for Setting and 
Managing Speed Limits in Ireland’.  
It is expected that the ‘Guidelines’ will be finalised by the start of  Quarter 4, this year. Subject to 
ministerial approval, it is envisaged that the updated ‘Guidelines’ will issue to local authorities with a 
direction to commence the process of reviewing existing speed limits in urban areas in their 
respective administrative areas, and to set appropriate speed limits in accordance with the 
Guidelines. 
 
The third and final stage deals with our National Secondary and Regional Roads. This phase is 
expected to start during 2026.
